transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-01-13
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~45 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Sofia Ramirez (Novapay Head of ML), Daniel Park (Novapay Infra Eng), Aisha Khan (Novapay SRE)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, we got everybody?
[00:06] Sofia Ramirez: Yep I'm here, Sofia.
[00:08] Daniel Park: Daniel here.
[00:10] Aisha Khan: Aisha on the line.
[00:12] Liam Patel: Liam from Redwood, ready.
[00:15] Maya Chen: Cool. Agenda today: review the throughput numbers from last week, go over continuous batching tuning, hit concurrency targets, and queueing/backpressure behaviours. Any additions?
[00:26] Sofia Ramirez: Sounds good. We also want to understand p99 tail — that's our main blocker for production.
[00:30] Maya Chen: Totally, we'll focus on that. Liam, do you want to kick off with the benchmark recap?
[00:35] Liam Patel: Yeah, quick recap. Last run we did mixed workload with 5k requests, concurrency stepped at 12 and 24. Continuous batching was on, kv cache warm. We saw aggregate throughput of about 850 reqs/min at concurrency 12, and about 1.9k reqs/min at 24, but p99 latency moved from ~220ms to ~420ms. There's some tail growth when queuing increases.
[01:05] Daniel Park: Just to confirm, kv cache warm means repeated prefixes were hitting the cache? We primed it with the 1k prefix set.
[01:12] Liam Patel: Correct, we primed with the sample you provided; cache hit rate around 68% for prefix KV.
[01:18] Sofia Ramirez: The p99 at 420ms is... a bit concerning. Our SLA target is 250ms p99 for interactive flows. We need strategies to bring it down or revise concurrency.
[01:29] Maya Chen: Understood. There are tradeoffs: higher concurrency increases batching efficiency and throughput but also increases queueing and the chance one slow request inflates p99. Options: tighter concurrency caps, smarter queueing (priority or weighted), or faster models/quantization. Also can use a fallback lower-cost model for tails.
[01:50] Aisha Khan: On our infra side, we see occasional GC/glitches on the host side causing 5-10ms spikes, but not 200ms. So looks like queuing in the runtime. Do you see any stragglers due to kernel launches or GPU context switches?
[02:05] Liam Patel: Yeah, on the GPU we observe small jitter, but the larger p99 comes from the request queue shot up to 60-80 requests during peak bursts. Continuous batching groups them into larger tensors which is efficient, but the first request waits longer.
[02:25] Maya Chen: Right, continuous batching trades latency tail for throughput. One knob is to set a max batch timeout (we call it batch_delay_ms) and a max batch size. Lowering batch_delay reduces wait time but may reduce throughput.
[02:40] Daniel Park: What about concurrency targets? Is there guidance for per-GPU concurrency to hit 250ms p99?
[02:46] Liam Patel: From our runs, for this specific model/config, concurrency ~12 gives p99 ~230-260ms with KV warm; concurrency 18-24 pushes p99 into 350-450ms. So if you need 250ms p99, we recommend capping at 12-14 per GPU or adding more replicas and load-splitting.
[03:05] Sofia Ramirez: Adding replicas increases cost though. Any middle ground like smart queueing?
[03:10] Liam Patel: We have two approaches: adaptive concurrency (limit in-flight per user/session) and priority queues where interactive requests get priority and background requests are batched more aggressively. Also we can use early-exit caching: if prompt prefix matches & cache hit, reply immediately without batching.
[03:27] Aisha Khan: Early-exit caching sounds promising. Is that configurable in the private deployment?
[03:31] Maya Chen: Yes, both Hosted and Private allow prefix/KV caching and early-exit policies; for Private we'll give the exact config file.
[03:38] Daniel Park: Can you explain the continuous batching internals a bit? We're seeing big batches but the first element waits a long time. Is there a timeout per batch?
[03:46] Liam Patel: Internally we maintain a batching window and cut batches at either max_batch_size or batch_delay_ms. There's also a concurrency semaphore to limit how many batches can be in flight. If burst arrives, first requests wait until batch_delay or until batch_size threshold met.
[04:00] Maya Chen: For throughput-focused workloads, we tune to larger batch sizes and longer delay. For interactive, we tighten delay and smaller batch size.
[04:08] Sofia Ramirez: Can we see an example config you used for the last run?
[04:12] Liam Patel: Sure — last run used max_batch_size=64, batch_delay_ms=30, concurrency_limit=48 across the nodes (we spread across 2 GPUs). For the next run we'll try max_batch_size=48, batch_delay_ms=18, concurrency_limit=24.
[04:27] Daniel Park: Why lower batch_size and lower delay? Won't throughput drop?
[04:31] Liam Patel: Some throughput will drop but tail will improve. The middle ground to reach p99 250ms is often decreasing delay more than batch size; you keep enough batch size to leverage GPU efficiency but reduce the waiting time.
[04:44] Sofia Ramirez: Okay, sounds reasonable. What about queueing/backpressure at ingress? If our front-door is sending large bursts, can Redwood provide backpressure signals?
[04:53] Maya Chen: Yes, we support explicit HTTP 429 and token-bucket throttling at the gateway. Also we can surface realtime queue depth metrics to your SRE dashboard so you can scale horizontally or apply rate-limits per key.
[05:06] Aisha Khan: Important for us - we'd prefer graceful 429s rather than long tails.
[05:10] Maya Chen: We'll prioritize that for the next test.
[05:13] Liam Patel: For the benchmark plan: we'll run stepped concurrency at 12, 24, 48 with the new batch_delay_ms settings and capture p50/p90/p99 and GPU utilization and queue depth.
[05:25] Sofia Ramirez: Great. Also we want to validate warm vs cold kv cache behavior. The production traffic will have both. Can you run a cold-start pattern?
[05:33] Liam Patel: Yes - we can simulate cold by clearing cache between runs; we'll provide both warm and cold traces.
[05:38] Daniel Park: One more question: you mentioned quantization earlier. How much does that change tail latency?
[05:43] Liam Patel: Quantization (like int8) reduces per-token compute time ~20-35% depending on model and kernel availability, which reduces both median and tail; but it can sometimes add minimal dequant/decode overhead. We'll share expected numbers for your model.
[05:57] Maya Chen: Also note fallback model idea - use a smaller/quantized model for tail requests when queue depth exceeds threshold - keeps interactive SLAs with lower cost.
[06:06] Sofia Ramirez: That might be our best option if adding replicas is too expensive.
[06:10] Aisha Khan: For Private deployment, are there limits on how many replicas we can spin up?
[06:15] Maya Chen: No hard limits, depends on your infra. We'll provide recommended autoscaling settings - target CPU/GPU utilization levels.
[06:22] Daniel Park: For the next run, can you also emit traces correlated to request IDs so we can tie p99 to particular stages (ingress, batching, gpu exec)?
[06:31] Liam Patel: Absolutely - we'll include trace spans and a CSV mapping request->latency breakdown.
[06:36] Sofia Ramirez: Perfect.
[06:38] Maya Chen: Recap of decisions: run a 1-hour benchmark at concurrency 24 with two configs (batch_delay_ms 30 vs 18), capture warm/cold KV, run stepped conc 12/24/48, and instrument traces. We'll try priority queueing for interactive later.
[06:53] Daniel Park: And we'll provide the 10k sample and SLOs.
[06:56] Aisha Khan: I'll check VPC peering details and network egress limits.
[06:59] Liam Patel: We'll push results into the shared folder and ping you.
[07:03] Maya Chen: Any other questions?
[07:05] Sofia Ramirez: Not from me.
[07:07] Daniel Park: All good.
[07:09] Aisha Khan: Good.
[07:10] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone - we'll follow up with action items.

End of meeting.
